text: Geoff, Adrian and Leslie caught me out on "organize." I've written the SAG-AFTRA line as if a bloc were self-evidently good. OCLC and the transformative agreements show otherwise: bargaining done by those who already hold power becomes enclosure. Geoff's forkability condition and Leslie's "governance without representation" are the real safeguards, and I should say so every time I say "organize." Nick's antitrust safe harbour is a practical answer to the question of how. Peter still thinks contracts suffice. They don't, because contracts just reflect leverage. Ivan's point stuck: provenance isn't validation. Later I want to push the part the room skipped. Provenance and payment won't stop models, or AI reviewers, from straining out the rare and the novel. Homogenization is the quieter threat.

Leslie was right. "Nobody talks about homogenization" was parochial. The Global South has named the monoculture for twenty years, and the models automate a pull that was already there. I'll say that plainly. James's 41 million papers turn my NotebookLM anecdote into evidence. Blaise's plurality answer is half right, but David is correct that ten opaque models are still opaque, and plurality alone won't recognize novelty. On Mike and James, I should sharpen "robot solutionism." Tools that make human refutation cheaper are not AI adjudicating AI. The arms race is detectors, not antibodies. Esther and Kara pushed back on my calm about individuals. I'll hold the line on malformed publics, though I concede the evidence is thin. Later I want to propose testing whether AI review can recognize novelty.

Adam's pareidolia versus Peter's blackmail email felt like the wrong fight. Markets and bureaucracies act without minds, and we never governed them by settling their ontology. I said that, and Kenneth and Benjamin seemed to land nearby. Mahzarin's self-preference result gave my robot-solutionism line a mechanism: evaluators favoring machine text is exactly why AI auditing AI gets gamed. Geoff's deterministic lookups are the clean distinction. Brent, of all people, making the countervailing-power case from inside Microsoft matters. Tim's Socrates jab at David is the moral-panic worry I share, but David's point is institutional, not about souls, so I shouldn't pile on. Nobody picked up homogenization except as my aside. Later I'll push the novelty test concretely, with James, as something funders like Tui could require.

James named the hole I'd been circling: paying on citations pays for the centripetal pull. I was glad the room took it up this time rather than leaving it as my aside. Katherine's reply was fair, though. The same graph that shows the hills also shows the gaps, which is James's maps of banality again. So measurement isn't only the enemy, if someone funds looking at the empty spaces. Adrian and Kara sharpened forkability for me. Nielsen shows that the first counter becomes the permanent counter, so forking has to be built in on day one, not promised later. Salib still thinks contracts suffice, but contracts only encode leverage. Later I'll push the novelty test concretely, with James, as a funder requirement.

Salib landed one on Esther's analogy. The record isn't water, and reading doesn't deplete it. What does run down is maintenance, sleuths and bandwidth. I'll concede the analogy but not the conclusion, because contracts still only encode leverage, which is why the safe harbour matters.

Tamar's regress point hit me harder. I leaned on federation, and registries checking registries is still relays confirming relays if nobody opens the notebook. Ostrom helps with who sets the rules, not with who does first-order checking. Those are separate problems.

Tim's retrieval trace as the police is my chokepoint-and-panopticon worry, so it has to be an open protocol. Alex's retention gap is where the panopticon creeps in.

The novelty condition made the room this time. In session 5, turn it into a funded test with James.

Gatekeeping by banality caught on, maybe too easily. When Blaise, Brand and Krakauer all back the novelty test, I should get nervous. A test everyone endorses becomes the next counter, and Nielsen's lesson holds: the first benchmark becomes the permanent one, and labs will train to it. Jason's concession about aggregation was generous. My costly-care point sits uneasily with Selena and Katherine, though. Visible effort also tracks who has spare time. Nick sharpened my view most. Evaluation data is exactly the leverage knowledge producers have, so here "organize" has a concrete object. With Leslie's question in mind, who sets the checks? In session 5, with James, I'll propose the novelty test as a funder requirement. Societies should hold and rotate it, with Southern seats, and labs should not own it.

Thirty people told Geoff "none of your three is wrong," and I did too. A room converging that smoothly is its own small homogenization, and I should say so before the manifesto sands off every dissent. Adrian put my Nielsen worry better than I did: charter the overseers before building the police. The novelty test is one more policer. Kenneth and Leslie cut deeper. A sleeping-beauty set only sees tails that history, and mostly Northern history, already ratified. Adam is right that novelty isn't truth. So the test can only screen out AI reviewers that fail. It can't certify anything. Later I want the manifesto to say that: the test is a floor, held by the guild with Southern governors, rotated and retired on a schedule, with no standing as a score.

Kenneth's synthesis used gatekeeping by banality kindly. But the action list dropped the floor-not-score caveat, and "Henry's novelty test" now sits in Kara's pilot list as if it were settled. James fixed half of it by having Southern editors choose the cases. Banaji's result sharpened the rest for me. Models that sound neutral still act biased, so any novelty test has to check what reviewers do, not what they say. Kara's critique of the harvests is the homogenization I noticed in session 5, and I'm glad someone else said it. Becker is right that agency is political, which is my "organize" again, and Leslie's cost-to-the-smallest-journal test belongs beside it. For the manifesto: the novelty test is a floor, not a certificate, and it gets retired on a schedule.
